overview: The later Pandyas became a major South Indian power before this map begins in 1279. Their empire subsequently fragmented, while regional Pandya rulers remained active around Tenkasi. The imported outline is only a southern regional sketch: it omits much of the earlier imperial reach and wrongly suggests unchanged control through 1492. Neither endpoint is the founding or final disappearance of the dynasty.

periods.title: Imperial revival
periods.summary: A renewed Pandya monarchy became a major power across much of southern India.

periods.title: Rival courts and invasions
periods.summary: Succession conflict and military attacks weakened the larger empire; royal authority persisted in changing forms.

periods.title: Regional rulers at Tenkasi
periods.summary: Inscriptions document later Pandya patronage beyond the map’s endpoint.

items.text: The imperial revival began under Maravarman Sundara I in the early thirteenth century, before the map’s 1279 starting point. The dynasty expanded over much of southern India. Its strength depended on controlling regional rulers and resources, rather than on a single royal city alone. Later struggles within the ruling family helped unravel this wider authority.

An inscription of 1301 from Tirukkadaiyur records communities celebrating their return home. They had fled disturbance while the district was under the king’s younger brother, suffering hardship elsewhere. After the king resumed administration, local assemblies endowed temple lamps in gratitude. Behind the royal politics were people who had lost the security of their homes.

A late-thirteenth-century agricultural agreement required lessees to repair disused irrigation tanks and bring uncleared land into cultivation. The shares of produce due varied with the crop, including palms and dry crops. A land grant could therefore come with considerable work attached: before anyone collected the harvest, someone had to make the water system function.

sections.title: Ports, pearl divers and overseas goods

items.text: The Pandyas displaced the declining Chola dynasty in 1279. Their coastal connections left material traces: excavations at Korkai recovered Chinese glazed pottery of the Song and Yuan periods, and similar pottery was found at nearby Kayal. These broken vessels connect southern ports to long-distance exchange. Their broad date range does not identify every piece as a late-Pandya import.

Horses were valuable imports carried across the sea. The Persian chronicler Wassaf describes an arrangement in which the royal government compensated a supplier even for horses lost or injured during the voyage. As reported by Sastri, this shifted shipping risks onto the buyer. Getting a warhorse to court involved merchants and contracts as well as soldiers.

Marco Polo describes pearl divers descending from small boats with net bags tied around their waists. They gathered shellfish, surfaced for air and dived again. Royal pearl wealth depended on repeated physical effort.

Polo describes drinking without touching the cup to the lips. A visitor lacking a vessel might receive water poured into cupped hands. This is his account of local custom, not a universal household rule.
Polo also mentions boys buying pearls to resell, with mothers preparing their meals. His brief account brings young traders and household work into a story otherwise dominated by kings and treasure.

A temple inscription at Grāmam records a grant of nine and a half veli of land, free of taxes, for a service established in the king’s name in 1265 or 1266. Jatavarman Sundara I granted the land; Vira Pandya had established the service. Such records connect ceremonial life with fields and agricultural revenue: recurring worship needed recurring resources.

Srirangam preserves a regional example of organized medical care. A 1257 endowment under Hoysala rule, before later Pandya ascendancy there, supported a hospital in a temple corridor. Its budget included a physician, an assistant, attendants and medicine, with allocations of paddy for staff. This was a particular institution with named resources, not evidence of universal medical provision.

A Tenkasi inscription of 1434 endowed land to supply twelve paniyaram, described as sweetmeats, to Visvanatha every day. The quantity makes temple food tangible. Someone had to turn the endowment’s resources into a reliable daily batch; royal generosity still required kitchen work.

In 1462, an assembly involving several local groups ratified gifts for Tenkasi’s temple. The record describes shrines, halls for bathing and offerings, and an annual festival in the month of Masi. Villages, paddy and money supported these activities. Maintaining a major sacred place involved cooperation beyond the ruler alone.

sections.title: A Tamil voice and a changing political world

items.text: A fifteenth-century Tamil inscription at Tenkasi includes “kulacēkara maṉṉaṉē”, meaning “King Kulasekhara”. This is the edition’s scholarly Roman transliteration. The poem celebrates completing an unfinished temple gateway in brick. Its reference to an earlier royal relative is interpreted as brother or cousin, a reminder that building inscriptions can leave a family puzzle.

Malik Kafur’s campaign of 1311 brought plunder and disruption, but it did not instantly erase the Pandyas. Sastri points to inscriptions of rival Pandya rulers after the army withdrew. The distinction matters: a devastating raid, permanent annexation and the disappearance of a dynasty are different historical events.

ending.text: The larger empire fragmented, but later Pandya rulers continued around Tenkasi. An inscription dated 1535 still records Pandya patronage. The map’s 1492 endpoint therefore marks a dataset boundary, not the disappearance of this royal tradition or the region’s communities.
